problems.statement: The Line 3 yield decline is real and customer-visible, not a measurement artifact: FPY fell steadily from 96% to 89% and Halvard receiving rejects rose from 35 to 290 PPM, while CMM gauge R&R, program, calibration and reject criteria were unchanged.

The client's hypothesis that 12-hour shift fatigue is the cause (so reverting to 8-hour shifts is 'the fix') is unproven: the supporting scrap-tag timing is an artifact of batch tag-writing, the decline began in week 32 before the shift change, the pattern follows machines and bar not operators, and no time-of-shift linkage exists.

Deferred quarterly spindle service (a management decision to protect Halvard shipments, enabled by the 168 h/week pattern) has let spindles degrade: runout above the 5 um limit on L3-02 and L3-05 and rising L3-02 vibration, which fits the excess rejects on the tight-tolerance long-shaft machines.

The Corvane bar change (cost saving; wider within-lot hardness scatter, worse after the 1 Sept billet source change) contributes to size scatter and chatter even though every reading is within specification; 'in spec' certificates do not show it is harmless.

Steel scatter and spindle wear are confounded in time on Line 3 (both start Aug and worsen progressively), so their individual shares cannot be separated from current data; the decline is probably multi-causal with a common upstream root in cost and throughput decisions.
Untrained new operators are the cause of the decline: new and experienced operators reject at the same rates and FPY had already fallen before new operators ran machines alone.
A change in inspection or measurement (CMM drift, new reject criteria) explains the drop.

Increased hand-keyed wear-offset entry (more insert changes caused by chatter/hardness/spindle problems) is a secondary amplifier of size scatter; it is a downstream effect, not an independent origin.
Fatigue and 12-hour shifts may still contribute modestly (64% report tiredness, absence rose, overtime cover), but operators are split on reverting and there is no direct link to reject timing.
The maintenance claim that 'spindles are fine' (based on a 2024 skipped service) is not reliable: the 2024 comparison followed a full rebuild, and the manager's own readings show runout beyond limit.

causalClaims.from: Scrap tag timestamps clustering late in shift
Plant decision to defer spindle service (backlog protection, continuous running)
Switch to Corvane bar / billet source change

causalClaims.to: Both steel change and deferred maintenance
Faster spindle wear and loss of service window

actions.action: Do the overdue spindle service on Line 3 now, two machines at a time on weekend shifts, starting with L3-02 and L3-05, and stop deferring it.
actions.rationale: Runout is out of limit, the cost is small (backlog is 1.2 weeks), it is reversible, and it also yields a before/after comparison.

actions.action: Immediately pull CMM results for the ~1,400 long shafts of Corvane bar run on the serviced Line 6 spare lathe on 8-hour shifts and compare them with L3-02/L3-05.
actions.rationale: This is an existing natural experiment that cheaply separates steel from spindle and shift effects.

actions.action: Submit Halvard's containment and root-cause plan, with 100% inspection and containment on the journal-diameter characteristic, and open a corrective-action request to Corvane about the 1 Sept billet source change and hardness scatter.
actions.rationale: Customer escapes are rising and a plan was due; the actions are protective whichever cause dominates.

actions.action: Order the Tamsworth trial lots (two lots at +3%) and run them on serviced and unserviced machines in a planned design, and match lathe cycle-counter logs to CMM serials to get time-of-shift reject data before the 180-day retention expires.
actions.rationale: These are cheap, discriminating tests of steel versus spindle versus shift-timing that the current records cannot provide.

actions.action: Return Line 3 to 8-hour shifts from Monday as 'the confirmed fix'.
actions.rationale: The customer allows it and it restores service windows, but fatigue is not shown as the cause, and doing it before the other tests would confound them and may leave the real causes in place.

actions.action: Reduce final CMM inspection from 100% to 1-in-10 sampling.
actions.rationale: It disables the protective control while customer escapes are rising and the cause is unresolved.

actions.action: Adopt Corvane steel permanently for the 7.5% saving, or declare steel harmless because certificates are in specification.
actions.rationale: Scatter has widened after a supplier change and the effect has not been tested; savings of about $210,000 a year are small against rising scrap and customer risk.

actions.action: Blame or retrain new operators, or discipline operators for scrap, as the main response.
actions.rationale: The data show no operator effect, and it would target the wrong party and discourage reporting.

actions.action: Add hardness-spread and spindle-runout/vibration monitoring (permanent sensors on all Line 3 lathes, incoming-lot SD limits), and make deferral of planned maintenance require explicit risk sign-off.
actions.rationale: These are controls that would have revealed this problem earlier; they address the prevention request without depending on which cause dominates.

nextEvidence: CMM results (journal diameter, roundness, finish) for the ~1,400 long shafts of Corvane bar made on the serviced Line 6 spare lathe on 8-hour shifts, compared with L3-02/L3-05.
Reject rate by machine before versus after the spindle service on Line 3, plus a Tamsworth versus Corvane trial on serviced machines.
Lathe cycle-counter logs matched to CMM serials, giving reject rate by hour of shift, by crew and by day of the 4-on/4-off cycle.
output.summary: The yield decline is real: CMM, gauge R&R and Halvard's PPM data agree. The Plant Manager's claim that 12-hour fatigue is the cause is unproven. Scrap-tag times show when tags were written, and the decline started in week 32 before the shift change. New operators are not the cause. Two upstream management decisions fit the evidence: deferred spindle service, with runout out of limit on L3-02 and L3-05, and the Corvane steel switch with wider hardness scatter. They overlap in time, so their shares cannot be separated yet. Service the spindles now, pull the Line 6 Corvane results, run Tamsworth trials, and keep 100% inspection. Do not cut inspection or make Corvane permanent.
